title: AC voltage applied to resistor, inductor, and capacitor
topicTitle: AC voltage applied to resistor, inductor, and capacitor
notes: When a sinusoidal voltage is applied to a pure resistor, the current follows the voltage with no delay. The rms current is the rms voltage divided by R, and the average power is the heating I_rms squared times R.

A pure inductor opposes a changing current. Its reactance is X_L = 2πfL, so a higher frequency or a larger inductance means a smaller current. The voltage leads the current by a quarter of a cycle, and the average power is zero.

A pure capacitor opposes a change of voltage. Its reactance is X_C = 1/(2πfC), which is large at low frequency and small at high frequency. The current leads the voltage by a quarter cycle, and again the average power is zero.
The three elements are drawn as phasors. The resistor voltage lies along the current. The inductor voltage is drawn 90° ahead of the current. The capacitor voltage is drawn 90° behind the current.
Household meters read rms values. A peak of 10√2 volts has an rms value of 10 V. Mixing a peak voltage with an rms current gives a wrong power.
A real coil is an inductor with resistance in series. The pure cases on this page are the pieces used later to build the impedance of an LCR circuit.

summary: A resistor takes an in-phase current and dissipates I_rms squared R. An inductor has reactance 2πfL and makes the voltage lead. A capacitor has reactance 1/(2πfC) and makes the current lead. Pure L and C exchange energy with the source and take no average power.
